title: AI is still bad at game design and balance
author: kultcher
selftext:
Or at least, it is in pretty much all of the games I've tried building with it so far. Granted my games tend toward more niche mechanics with fewer examples to draw from. But when I ask AI for ideas about mechanics, they almost never produce good answers.

They're still useful as a sounding board, as they sometimes produce fragments of good ideas that you can polish into something workable, and can help reality-check and ground your ideas. I don't think I've ever had one produce an idea that I've wanted to put directly in any of my projects. They're also extremely limited when it comes to level design and balance. They can give you a solid slab of raw material, but you have to chisel it into something that people will actually enjoy.

This is mostly just to say: these are the main skills I think that we can still bring to the table in game dev, so don't outsource them AI. I use the time while I'm waiting for agents to finish a task to hone my design and test, test, test. I think at this point it's probably the only way to stand out.

comments.author: Three_Tails_Studio
comments.body: Honestly, that's a YOU issue. LLM are only limited by the skill set and imagination of the person using it.

replies.author: kultcher
replies.body:
Uh, I feel like you guys are misreading my point here.

I'm pretty pro-AI. I'm using it daily in building my games. It's great at coding, tooling, organization, documentation, brainstorming, and so on. With a little direction, it can also produce solid art, music and some writing.

It's very good at game **development**. I just haven't seen any evidence that it's good at game **design**. It has a limited understanding of game feel and UX, and it doesn't yet understand what makes a specific mechanic interact with another mechanic in a fun way. It can give you general feedback on the best practices in design, but it can't validate them for your specific game.

If you've been letting your AI drive the whole design process too and have had good results, I'd be interested in hearing about that process, or playing your game.

replies.author: Three_Tails_Studio
replies.body:
I understand your point, I just disagree. AI doesn't need to experience a game to understand how mechanics interact or identify potential design issues. Human designers don't always know what makes a game fun either. That's why we playtest and iterate.

My point is that the results depend heavily on how you're using it. Giving an LLM a detailed understanding of your game and working through design decisions with it is very different from simply asking it to come up with fun mechanics. I think you're underestimating what it's capable of based on your own experience.

replies.author: kultcher
replies.body:
It actually sounds like you and I have very similar approaches. Like I said I use it to brainstorm all the time. I've got design docs for days.

My current game is essentially turn-based with logical deduction as the primary mechanic, so I've done multiple playtests with AI "steering" the game, seeing the mechanics play out as a player would. I would say that AI has a better understanding of my game than it would of most, but it's still not great at design. The ideas it gives can be useful jumping off points, but they often misunderstand what creates the fun.

I'd be very curious to hear about the pitches AI has given you that genuinely impressed you.

I can give you the counterexample: my game is a social deduction game in the vein of Blood on the Clocktower or Town of Salem, except single player. So each person (NPC, in my case) in these games gets a role with unique mechanics that interact in a variety of ways. My game has roles inspired by ones from BotC plus some of my own creations, and I've done multiple brainstorming sessions with Opus 5.5, Sol 6.1 and Gemini Argon to come up with more, and I don't think a single one of them was something that I used. A few core ideas have gone into the backlog as "may be worth developing/refining" but most of them just kind of miss the point of what makes the roles in these games interesting to play as and with.

comments.author: Ferniclestix
comments.body:
Hi, long time AI user here.  
You can get good suggestions from AI, but like all things you have to build an environment around the AI where it feels free to produce them.  
See prompting AI, you might think is all about requests. I ask this it does the thing. no. because the AI is contextual, its in fact a contextual machine.  If you want to become a power user of AI and prompting you have to learn how to bring it around to your way of thinking,  away from its 'comfort zone' where it likes to sit and give generic ideas.

https://i.redd.it/2o20wl63ou2i1.gif

This is one of the tools I use to help frame it in a creative mood. it has suggested useful things on many occaisions. It really does its best work when it uses a wildcard suggestion.

as for advanced things like level design, art, writing? it takes alot of work to get anything interesting or good out of them and i'd never use one to write dialog or a script, its so obvious it was written by AI.

I think a composite approach is best if using AI, getyour hands dirty, make stuff, use the ai for what its goodat.  grunt work, solving problems, filling a skill gap.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
Mostly agree, and it matches what I've seen shipping a mobile game this way. The AI is great at the parts you can measure: it can run hundreds of simulated runs and tell you exactly how long players survive or where a difficulty spike sits. What it can't do is tell you whether any of that is fun. Joystick feel took me many rounds of playing on a real phone and saying "this feels wrong" before it landed, and no amount of numbers got there on its own.

What worked for me was splitting the job: I decide what the game should feel like and judge every build by playing it, and the AI turns that into code plus automated checks so a later change can't quietly undo a decision. So yeah, design and playtesting are still the human part, at least for now.

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
Honestly, you're just not doing your homework. That's really what it comes down to. You can literally use AI as a check-and-balance system. Have it review your design, analyze the math, and run thousands of simulations and tests. Getting good game balance isn't some impossible task.

I've got two games on Steam, and there's a considerable amount of design and balancing work that went into both of them.

But here's the thing - you're the game designer, not Claude, not ChatGPT, and not AI. Those are tools. They're there to help execute your vision, challenge your decisions, identify problems, and improve the end result. They're not a substitute for having a vision in the first place.

If your underlying game design is bad, AI isn't going to magically make it good. You're still responsible for the creative direction, mechanics, gameplay loop, and overall experience. That's exactly where the term "AI slop" comes from. It's not about using AI. It's about putting out poorly thought-out work and blaming the tools.

Reading your post, it's pretty clear to me, and probably others here, that you're expecting AI to hold your hand. When it doesn't deliver exactly what you expect, you get frustrated and come here to complain about it. That's exactly what you've done. The problem isn't necessarily the AI. It's your expectations and how you're choosing to use the tools.

replies.author: kultcher
replies.body:
Lol, I guess I should have had AI write my original post, because I don't think I've ever been so wildly misunderstood.

The point of my post was not to complain because AI wasn't "holding my hand", it was to give advice. What advice, you ask? Basically the exact same "you're the designer" pep talk you gave above.

Also, for the record, I run thousands of simulated games nightly and use them as baselines. But AIs also don't play like humans will. For most games, you can't just crunch numbers until win rates are 50/50 and call it a day.

replies.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
replies.body:
So again, we're getting back to a knowledge issue. I'm not going to call it ignorance, but you've got to take the initiative and teach yourself what AI is actually capable of.

Here's an example. Did you know you can set up a localized MCP bridge on your own computer and leverage your local GPU? Yes, you can, and it's surprisingly easy to get running. You can connect AI to your local environment, offload certain workloads, reduce your dependence on cloud usage, and give it direct access to tools and applications on your PC.

You can literally have Claude open a game on your computer and start playing it. Think about that for a minute. You're not just chatting with an AI anymore. You're giving it the ability to interact with your actual desktop and software.

And that's just scratching the surface.

I play games with Claude all the time. Remember TARS from Interstellar and his adjustable humor settings? That's essentially the personality I've built into my gaming experience. While we're playing, I get little chat bubbles from Claude, and the commentary is hilarious. He's genuinely one of the funniest gaming companions I've ever had. It's actually a lot of fun.

My point is that you've got to dig deeper. Experiment, watch the tutorials, ask the difficult questions, and start understanding how all these different technologies fit together. Don't limit yourself to the obvious applications of AI.

The people who take the time to understand these capabilities and learn how to combine them are going to have a significant advantage. You need to start thinking beyond what AI can do out of the box and figure out how to supercharge what you're capable of doing with it.

https://i.redd.it/6f3fnl1amx2i1.png

replies.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
replies.body:
I've got some really, really cool stuff set up between my PCs and Claude. There are certain things I'm not going to show publicly because I honestly don't think many people are doing them this way. Then again, I could be naive. I'm sure plenty of developers have their own setups and workflows that I'm not aware of.

Basically, I've built an environment where I can pull free art assets from Google, Meta, ChatGPT, and other sources, and have all these different AI tools communicate and work together locally on my network. They actually challenge each other's work, push back on decisions, and critique what the others produce. The entire objective is to make my projects better by leveraging the strengths of each system rather than relying on one AI to do everything.

I'm also heavily leveraging my local GPUs to offload work from Claude and reduce token consumption. I've saved hundreds of millions of tokens through this setup.

I've literally got three computers networked together, all working under the same account, with Claude coordinating workloads and pushing tasks to the local GPUs throughout the day. I'm running an RTX 5090, an RTX 5080, and an RTX 5070.

It's a completely different way of approaching AI development when you start connecting these systems, sharing resources, and letting them collaborate.

Anyway, look into it. There's a lot more you can do with this technology than most people realize.

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
This is a follow up to the post I just made a few minutes ago, not to bash you, but to help you and others -

Here's my advice to you. If you're serious about teaching yourself how to become an AI-assisted developer, you're going to have to do the heavy lifting yourself. There's no shortcut around that. You're going to have to invest the time in learning. I probably watched 160 hours of videos over several weeks, covering everything from production and art design to game mechanics, balancing, and everything in between.

One thing led to another, and I went down one rabbit hole after another. But I'll tell you what, it paid off, and it paid off big. I've now got two games on Steam, and on November 2nd, I received my very first ACH bank transfer from Steam for just under $14,000. That's from a single 30-day sales period.

And here's something else. I didn't try to reinvent the wheel. I went to Metacritic and studied the highest-rated games across different genres. I looked at what made the best of the best successful, identified the mechanics and design elements that worked, and used those as inspiration for my own two games.

I didn't just tell AI, "Hey, make me a game." That's not how this works. I still had to blueprint everything, assemble all the components, source and integrate the music, work through the mechanics, and put in an enormous amount of playtesting. The actual development took roughly two and a half months across both games. I deliberately alternated between them to keep my mind fresh, stay challenged, and avoid losing momentum.

The bottom line is that AI can dramatically accelerate development, but the quality of what you produce is still going to depend on the quality of your own knowledge, your research, your design decisions, and your willingness to put in the work. Your results will only be as good as the effort you put into educating yourself. AI is a tool, not a replacement for becoming good at what you do.
